Comment: Seen for about 15 seconds in the meadow with the creek running through it approximately halfway between Cameron Line and Blezard Line (exact location: 44.297750, -78.090547). Unfortunately I did not see it perched and I did not get a photo. After looking at several field guides and many photos online I don't think it could be anything else. What I noted in the field: very large sulphur (noticeably much larger than Clouded or Orange Sulphur), bright yellow overall with no visible orange, no black visible on dorsal surface of wings, very rapid flight (quite different flight pattern than the regular Sulphurs we see here). The presence of a Little Yellow which we found a bit later indicates that there has likely been some butterfly migration.

Remarks: With Wilderness Birding Adventures, Aaron Lang, leader
Comment: Apologies, but I originally identified this as "Freija" - but the dorsal pattern is wrong.  Dorsal pattern is either "chariclea" or "polaris" - However, Polaris flies beginning of June, (Arctic Fritillary is late June, July) and considering how far north we are, and how worn this bug is, a worn Polaris seems more likely.  Also, Polaris is known for its white HW chevrons along the marginal band. So those white chevrons are not due to wear, but a remnant of the actual dorsal color.

Comment: This is one of the most unusual satyrs I have photographed. I am leaning towards intricata due to the extreme patternless nature of the forewing and hindwing, very different from the Carolina satyrs I photographed at this location. This individual did not have the bulging vein described in Warren et al. 2014, but they did consider this feature as variable. Feedback would be appreciated. I suppose without capturing the butterfly and examining genitalia I will never be positive.

Often there were multiple catepillars feeding on a leaf.  Approximately one third of the leaves on each milkweed plant were occupied by tent catepillars who had rolled the leaves up for pupation.  Many newly emerged adult tent catepillars were also present on the rolled up leaves.  It's been a 'bad' year for tent catepillars with large swathgs of forest in the area being heavily defoliated.

Comment: Surprise! Un papilionidé sp. d'une espèce qui nous est inconnue. Nous avons fait une recherche parmi les espèces nord-américaine et ne l'avons pas trouvé. Peut-être est-ce un échappé de captivité ou un individu égaré loin de son aire? Environ 10 cm d'envergure, il était un peu plus grand qu'un Papillon tigré du Canada (Papilio canadensis). Il butinait des fleurs d'Asclépiade commune (Asclepias syriaca) sur le bord de notre maison. Quelques photographies ont été prises.
